meta.dataset_name: Black History Discovery Dataset (HubHacks 2026 proof of concept)
meta.description: Metadata and links only, for a discovery layer built for the Black Cultural Centre for Nova Scotia (BCCNS). Each record is one institution's description of a Black history resource. The platform does not copy collections: it holds short curator-written descriptions plus the authoritative source_url, and sends users to the institution that supplies the description (record_source_id) and, where known, the institution that holds the original (holding_institution_id). Reuse scope for every record is metadata_and_link_only.

record.title_original: Book of Negroes
record.description: Nova Scotia Archives' online presentation of the British copy of the 1783 Book of Negroes, a register of about 3,000 Black refugees who sailed from New York to Nova Scotia between April and November 1783. You can page through digitized images of the register, which is held in the UK.
record.content_note: Title uses historical terminology now considered offensive; retained as written by the source.
record.container_title: African Nova Scotians in the Age of Slavery and Abolition
record.notes: NSA says two originals were made at the same time. The British one (shown here) is at The National Archives, Kew. The American one is at the US National Archives in Washington, and NSA holds microfilm of it (nos. 23164 and 23165). The page also explains historical place names (St. Johns = Saint John NB; Port Roseway = Shelburne; Fort Cumberland near Amherst).
record.holder_note: The NSA landing page says the British version is in the "Sir Guy Carlton papers at the Public Records Office" (spelled Carlton there), reference PRO 30/55/100. Equating the Public Records Office with today's The National Archives (Kew) is our identification. Every image page is captioned "Guy Carleton, 1st Baron Dorchester: Papers, The National Archives, Kew (PRO 30/55/100)" (spelled Carleton). TNA's own story page uses the same reference and points to Discovery C3070438, which could not be rendered.
record.access_instructions: Page through the register images with the previous/next links from the landing page. The original is at The National Archives, Kew (PRO 30/55/100).
record.rights_statement: Page contents are Crown copyright, Province of Nova Scotia. Personal, non-commercial use of web images is allowed. Commercial, educational or media use needs a Rights Declaration and an Image Use Request to NSA. Credit the Nova Scotia Archives.
record.change_notes: Split from SRC-001 (v1), which had merged the NSA and LAC descriptions. The v1 title "Book of Negroes, 1783" is LAC's form; NSA labels it "Book of Negroes". v1 reference "Guy Carleton papers, PRO 30/55/100" is now source_reference "PRO 30/55/100". CONFLICT (kept NSA's range): date ranges differ across sources. NSA gives 23 April–30 November 1783, LAC gives April–November 1783, and TNA gives 15 April 1783–19 February 1784 (the TNA range includes later board hearings and a London signing). The date_display wording comes from a WebFetch summary; check it by eye.

record.title_original: Book of Negroes, 1783
record.description: Library and Archives Canada's searchable name index of the British copy of the 1783 Book of Negroes. It covers about 3,000 Black men, women and children who left New York for Nova Scotia, searchable by details such as age, gender, place of origin and ship.
record.content_note: Title uses historical terminology now considered offensive; retained as written by the source. LAC also gives a historical language advisory: some racial descriptors in the register entries are considered offensive today.
record.notes: LAC calls the Book of Negroes a small part of the British Headquarters Papers. It presents the database under "Carleton Papers - Loyalists and British Soldiers, 1772 to 1784". The database is a transcription made from microfilm of the British version, not page images. About 800 entries have no surname. LAC says the American version is at the US National Archives and Records Administration.
record.holder_note: LAC's page says the British version is held at the UK National Archives as part of the Carleton Papers. It gives no TNA reference number. PRO 30/55/100 comes from the NSA and TNA pages (see SRC-001a).
record.access_instructions: Search LAC's transcribed database with the "Search the Book of Negroes, 1783" link on the page. The advanced keyword field accepts age, gender, place of origin or ship. To see the record itself, view the microfilm in person at LAC in Ottawa, order copies, or hire a researcher. Page images of the British original are on the Nova Scotia Archives site.
record.rights_statement: Government of Canada material. Accurate, credited non-commercial reproduction needs no permission. Commercial redistribution needs written permission from LAC.
record.change_notes: Split from SRC-001 (v1). The LAC page shows no PRO/MG reference or reel number, so PRO 30/55/100 was not carried here. Page date modified 2026-10-01. The search database URL was not visible in the fetched content. CONFLICT (kept LAC's wording): the Book of Negroes date range differs across NSA, LAC and TNA (see SRC-001a). The "April to November 1783" label comes from a WebFetch summary; check it by eye.

record.holder_note: The citation on the page reads "Commissioner of Public Records, Nova Scotia Archives, RG 1 volume 170 page 333 (microfilm 15282)".
record.access_instructions: The document image is on the page. For the original or microfilm at the Archives, cite RG 1 vol. 170 p. 333 / microfilm 15282.
record.rights_statement: Crown copyright, Province of Nova Scotia. Personal, non-commercial use is allowed. Other uses need an NSA Image Use Request; credit the Nova Scotia Archives.

record.title_original: A New Map of Nova Scotia, compiled...for the Historical & Statistical Account of Nova Scotia
record.description: An 1829 map of Nova Scotia, published as an illustration in Thomas Chandler Haliburton's historical account of the province. It marks Black settlements including Birchtown, Preston, Upper Hammonds Plains and Boydville.
record.container_title: African Nova Scotians in the Age of Slavery and Abolition

record.title_original: Letter From Lord Dalhousie to Earl Bathurst about the black refugees
record.description: A December 1816 letter in which Nova Scotia's lieutenant governor, Lord Dalhousie, reports to Earl Bathurst on the Black Refugees in Nova Scotia. It records a dismissive official view of their prospects.
record.content_note: The source page quotes period official language that describes Black refugees in demeaning terms. It is not reproduced here.
record.container_title: African Nova Scotians in the Age of Slavery and Abolition
record.notes: Lord Dalhousie is the writer. The page gives his term as lieutenant governor as 1816 to 1820.
record.holder_note: The citation on the page reads "Commissioner of Public Records, Nova Scotia Archives, RG 1 volume 112 pages 6-9 (microfilm 15262)". This is probably NSA's letterbook/copy volume; whether it is the sent original or a retained copy is not stated.
record.access_instructions: Images of the letter are on the page. To request it at the Archives, cite RG 1 vol. 112 pp. 6-9 / microfilm 15262.
record.rights_statement: Crown copyright, Province of Nova Scotia. Personal, non-commercial use is allowed. Other uses need an NSA Image Use Request; credit the Nova Scotia Archives.
record.change_notes: Title, date and reference confirmed. The page uses a hyphen in "6-9", not the en dash in v1. Recipient recorded as "Earl Bathurst" without a first name, because the page gives none. The full name George Ramsay, 9th Earl of Dalhousie, is our identification of "Lord Dalhousie"; it is not on the page.

record.title_original: Rose Fortune National Historic Person (circa 1774-1864)
record.description: Parks Canada's national historic person profile of Rose Fortune, a Black Loyalist who settled in Annapolis Royal. There she ran a baggage-carting business and informally kept order on the waterfront.

record.title_original: Thomas Peters National Historic Person (c. 1738–1792)
record.description: Parks Canada's profile of Thomas Peters, a Black Pioneer and Black Loyalist leader. He petitioned in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and London for land promised to Black Loyalists, and helped lead the 1792 migration from Halifax to Sierra Leone, where he died.
record.notes: The page says he is believed to have been born around 1738. It says he was designated in 2022, while the backgrounder refers to a 2023 ministerial announcement (the news release is dated February 2023). Page metadata issue date 2021-09-23. John Clarkson is not named on this page. This record keeps its SRC- ID by Owen's decision (2026-11-06) although it is a person profile.

record.title_original: Loyalists
record.description: Library and Archives Canada's research guide to Loyalist records (military, Loyalist lists, land and settlement, published sources). It includes pointers for Black Loyalist research such as the Book of Negroes and the 1784 Birchtown muster book.
record.content_note: The page carries LAC's historical language advisory: older records may use language about Black Canadians now considered offensive.
record.notes: A broad Loyalist guide, not a Black-history-only resource. It links to LAC's Book of Negroes, 1783 page, a "Black Loyalist refugees, 1782 to 1807" (Port Roseway Associates) page, and the Black Canadians guide. It cites the Shelburne records (MG9 B9 14), with 1,498 references to the "Muster Book of Free Black Settlement of Birchtown, Port Roseway, 1784".
record.access_instructions: Use the guide to find records. Some are digitized (Collection Search, Canadiana Héritage microfilm; Audit Office claims also on Ancestry.ca, free at LAC and many libraries). Others need a visit to LAC in Ottawa, a copy order, or a hired researcher.
record.rights_statement: Government of Canada material. Accurate, credited non-commercial reproduction needs no permission. Commercial redistribution needs written permission from LAC.
record.change_notes: Title, scope and access confirmed. Added the content_note (historical language advisory on the page) and the Port Roseway/Shelburne places. Page date modified 2026-10-01.

record.title_original: Portia May White (1911-1968) National Historic Person
record.description: Parks Canada's profile of Portia May White, a contralto from Nova Scotia's Black community. She was the first African-Canadian woman to win international recognition as a concert singer, after 1940s debuts in Toronto and New York.
record.notes: Designated 1995; HSMBC approved the plaque text in 1997. Plaque at 454 Prince Street, Truro (Zion United Baptist Church in the plaque photo). Trained with Dr. Ernesto Vinci at the Halifax Conservatory. Portrait © Yousuf Karsh / Library and Archives Canada / PA-192783, a possible link to a future LAC record.

record.title_original: Mary Ann Shadd National Historic Person (1823-1893)
record.description: Parks Canada's profile of Mary Ann Shadd, a Delaware-born advocate for Black refugees in 1850s Upper Canada. In 1853 she founded The Provincial Freeman, which promoted self-reliance and civil rights for Black people and women.
record.notes: Designated November 1994; HSMBC approved the plaque text in 2005. Plaque at 177 King Street East, Chatham, Ontario. The page points to digitized copies of The Provincial Freeman hosted by University of Pennsylvania Libraries. Photo © National Archives of Canada / C-29977.
record.access_instructions: Read the profile online.
record.rights_statement: Government of Canada content. Non-commercial reuse with credit is allowed. Images are third-party (National Archives of Canada photo; Wang Qijun illustration).
record.change_notes: Title confirmed with a hyphen. Added designation November 1994. Removed the separate "Delaware" and "Ontario" places (Delaware is the disambiguator for Wilmington; Ontario appears only in the plaque address). Page date modified 2023-10-10.

record.title_original: John Ware (circa 1850–1905) National Historic Person
record.description: Parks Canada's profile of John Ware, a cowboy likely born enslaved in the American South, who came to the District of Alberta on an 1882 cattle drive. He built a respected ranching career in southern Alberta, at Sheep Creek and later on the Red Deer River.
record.notes: Designated 2022. The page says his early life is unclear and that he was likely enslaved in the American South. Married Mildred Lewis in 1892; both died in 1905. Plaque at Bar U Ranch National Historic Site, Longview, Alberta. Photos are credited to University of Calgary collections.
record.access_instructions: Read the profile online.
record.rights_statement: Government of Canada content. Non-commercial reuse with credit is allowed. Photos are third-party (University of Calgary).

record.title_original: Harriet Tubman (circa 1822-1913) National Historic Person
record.description: Parks Canada's profile of Harriet Tubman, who escaped slavery in Maryland in 1849 and returned repeatedly to guide others north. From 1851 to 1858 she was based in St. Catharines, Canada West, where she was active in the abolition movement.
record.notes: Designated 2005; HSMBC approved the plaque text in 2011. The H1 gives circa 1822, but the body text says she was born in Maryland in 1820 or 1821, and the plaque gives c. 1822–1913. Plaque at 92 Geneva Street, St. Catharines. The page names the Refugee Slaves' Friends Society of St. Catharines (1852) and the Anti-Slavery Society of Canada. Salem Chapel appears only in related links.
record.access_instructions: Read the profile online.
record.rights_statement: Government of Canada content. Non-commercial reuse with credit is allowed. Images are third-party (Paul Collins; Library of Congress; National Portrait Gallery; Wang Qijun).

record.description: Saskatchewan heritage-property record for the log church built in 1912 by Black settlers who came from Oklahoma in 1910, and for the cemetery beside it. It explains why the site is significant and lists the features that protect its heritage character.

record.title_original: PRESTON, RICHARD
record.description: Dictionary of Canadian Biography entry on Richard Preston (1791 or 1792 to 1861), a Baptist minister and abolitionist. Born enslaved in Virginia, he bought his freedom and came to Nova Scotia to find his mother among the Black refugees of the War of 1812. He was ordained in London in 1832, led the African Chapel on Cornwallis Street in Halifax, formed the African Abolition Society, and founded the African Baptist Association in 1854.
record.notes: Biography by Frank S. Boyd Jr. First published 1985, revised 2023 (per the page's citation table). The portrait on the page is credited to the History Collection, Nova Scotia Museum (P149.29), via Nova Scotia Archives.

record.title_original: HALL, WILLIAM (baptized William Neilson) (1829-1904)
record.description: Dictionary of Canadian Biography entry on William Hall (1829 to 1904), a sailor and farmer from the Avon River area of Nova Scotia whose father was one of the Black refugees of the War of 1812. Serving in the Royal Navy, he was honoured for his part at Lucknow in November 1857 and received the Victoria Cross in 1859: the first Black person, the first Nova Scotian and the first Canadian sailor to receive it. The entry also describes memorials to him, several created by Nova Scotia's Black community.
record.content_note: The biography uses the colonial-era name "Indian Mutiny" for the 1857 uprising in India.
record.notes: Biography by Bridglal Pachai, published 1994. The page notes several suggested birth dates and places, all in Nova Scotia; this record uses the page's own dates. Images on the page are credited to the Maritime Museum of the Atlantic and Canada Post.
